raw_text:
Below is a 12-week postpartum return-to-exercise programme designed to start at four weeks after an uncomplicated C‑section with OB clearance for light activity only (walking, no abdominal work, no heavy lifting until 6‑week check). The plan assumes home training only (yoga mat available). The programme is conservative and progressive, focussed on restoring aerobic fitness, pelvic floor and deep core re‑education, mobility, posture, and then gradual return to strength and functional movement after the six‑week check. Emphasise symptom monitoring (pain, heaviness/bulging at incision or lower abdomen, urinary leakage, pelvic pressure, or increasing back pain). If any worrying signs appear, stop and refer back to the OB or to a pelvic health physiotherapist.

Programme overview
- Weeks 1–2 (current weeks 4–5 postpartum): Gentle reconditioning — walking progression, pelvic floor awareness, diaphragmatic breathing, gentle hip/mid-back mobility. No abdominal exercises or loading.
- Weeks 3–4 (weeks 6–7 postpartum, after 6‑week check): Begin gentle core reconnection and low-load strength work (bodyweight), continue walking progression. Introduce pelvic floor exercises with progression.
- Weeks 5–8 (weeks 8–11 postpartum): Progressive strengthening through bodyweight and light functional exercises, increase aerobic work (brisk walking, intervals), introduce more dynamic core integration (no heavy valsalva).
- Weeks 9–12 (weeks 12–15 postpartum): Build strength and conditioning, increase intensity and volume, reintroduce more loaded/impact activities if cleared and asymptomatic. Prepare for return to typical activities.

Key safety notes (to give your client and monitor each session)
- Stop and seek professional advice if she experiences: new or worsening incision pain, separation or bulging at incision or midline (diastasis recti gap increasing), pelvic heaviness/pressure, urinary or fecal leakage, or severe back/hip pain.
- Teach diaphragmatic breathing and pelvic floor cueing before any strengthening. Avoid breath‑holding/strain. Use gentle exhale during effort and continuous breathing.
- Progress only if asymptomatic, good quality movement, and no increased pelvic symptoms after activity (monitor for 24–48 hours).
- Encourage adequate sleep (as feasible), hydration, and protein intake to support recovery. Aim for ~20–25 g protein per meal/snack if possible and a balanced diet; specific calorie targets can be given if you request them.
- Fortify posture and ergonomics for baby handling; lift with legs once cleared for heavier lifting and avoid prolonged forward flexed positions.

Detailed week‑by‑week plan

Weeks 1–2 (postpartum weeks 4–5): Foundations — walking, pelvic floor re‑education, gentle mobility
Goal: Restore gentle aerobic base, re‑establish pelvic floor and breathing patterns, improve mobility and posture. No abdominal crunching/straining.

Frequency: 5 days/week light activity. 3 short focused mat sessions per week (20–25 minutes). Daily walking.

Daily walking
- Start with 10–20 minutes easy walking on flat ground once per day in week 1. Increase to 20–30 minutes per day by end of week 2 if comfortable. Keep heart rate light — able to talk without breathlessness.

Pelvic floor and breathing (every day)
- Diaphragmatic breathing with pelvic floor awareness (supine, knees bent): 5 minutes, 8–10 slow breaths. Inhale to expand belly/ribs, exhale gently draw pelvic floor slightly up and in (not hard squeeze), then relax. Repeat 6–8 reps per set, 2 sets.
- Pelvic floor “light lift” (submaximal) 6–8 slow contractions, hold 3–5 seconds, rest equal time; progress to 10 reps as tolerated. 3 sets per day. Avoid bearing down.

Mat session A — 3×/week (20–25 minutes)
- Warm up (5 minutes): seated breathing, neck/breath mobility, shoulder rolls, gentle cat/cow in neutral range (avoid deep ab doming).
- Hip bridges (glute activation): 2 sets of 8–10 reps, slow, focus on glute squeeze and neutral pelvis.
- Side‑lying clam (glute med): 2 sets of 10 reps per side.
- Bird‑dog progressions (from hands/knees only reach opposite arm then opposite leg): 2 sets 6 reps per side, slow and controlled.
- Seated heel slides (core reconnection, very gentle): 2 sets 8 per side — only if no doming or bulging.
- Gentle thoracic rotation (seated or supine, knees bent): 2 sets 8 per side.
- Cool down: pelvic floor breathing 2 minutes.

Recovery/nutrition cues
- Aim for protein at each meal (20–30 g) and stay hydrated, particularly if breastfeeding. Light anti-inflammatory foods and fiber to avoid constipation. Sleep when possible.

Weeks 3–4 (postpartum weeks 6–7): Start low‑load strength after 6‑week clearance
Goal: Introduce controlled core reconnection, increase walking intensity, add more targeted strength for hips, upper back and shoulders. Continue pelvic floor work.

Frequency: 4–5 days/week combined walking + 3 targeted mat/strength sessions per week (25–35 min).

Walking/aerobic work
- Progress to 30–40 minutes brisk walking 3–5 times per week. Add 1 session with gentle intervals: 1 minute quicker pace / 2 minutes easy x 6, if tolerated.

Pelvic floor progressions
- Continue diaphragmatic breathing daily. Pelvic floor holds: 3 sets of 8 holds x 6–8 seconds with full relaxation between. Add 10 quick contractions x 2 sets once per day as tolerated.

Mat/Strength sessions (three distinct sessions, rotate)
Session B — Core reconnection & posterior chain
- Warm up 5 minutes: breathing, scapular mobilizations, pelvic tilts.
- Bridge with march (glute dominant): 3 sets x 8–10 march steps total (alternate legs), focus on pelvic stability.
- Wall push‑ups (standing): 3 sets x 8–12 reps.
- Seated band row substitute (if no band: prone T’s on mat lifting arms): 3 sets x 10–12.
- Bird‑dog 3 sets x 8 per side.
- Side plank knees down progress (isometric): 2 sets x 10–20 seconds per side.
- Cool down breathing.

Session C — Lower body & balance
- Warm up 5 minutes.
- Supported split squat (reverse lunge to small range, hold onto chair): 3 sets x 8 per leg.
- Glute bridge single‑leg assist (foot elevated on chair, small range if needed): 3 sets x 6–8 per leg.
- Standing hip abduction (to side, control): 3 sets x 12 per side.
- Calf raises double‑leg: 3 sets x 12–15.
- Pelvic floor breathing finish.

Session D — Mobility & upper body
- Warm up 5 minutes.
- Wall slides for shoulder mobility: 3 sets x 10.
- Prone Y/T (lying on belly, lift arms small amounts) or seated scapular retraction: 3 sets x 8–10.
- Dead bug (very gentle, only if no doming): 2 sets x 8 per side — keep small range and bracing lightly on exhale.
- Hip flexor gentle stretch, child's pose modified for comfort.
- Pelvic floor breathing.

Progress rules: If she notices any bulging/pressure or leakage after sessions, reduce intensity and revert to earlier work; consult pelvic health physio.

Weeks 5–8 (postpartum weeks 8–11): Build strength and endurance; more dynamic core integration
Goal: Move toward higher volume strength, progressive overload using bodyweight, add variety to aerobic work.

Frequency: 4 strength sessions per week (30–40 minutes), 3–4 walks (30–45 min), could mix brisk walks + one longer walk or easy low‑impact cardio like stair stepping.

Strength structure: Two lower‑body focused, one upper‑body focused, one full‑body/core integration per week. Continue pelvic floor work 4–5 times/week.

Example weekly layout:
- Mon: Strength Lower A
- Tue: Walk 35–40 min brisk
- Wed: Strength Upper
- Thu: Rest or gentle walk
- Fri: Strength Lower B
- Sat: Active recovery walk or mobility session
- Sun: Strength Full‑body + core integration

Lower A (moderate difficulty)
- Warm up 5–7 min.
- Split squat (no support or light support): 3 sets x 10 per leg.
- Glute bridge single leg (if stable): 3 sets x 8 per leg.
- Hip hinge (Romanian bodyweight or suitcase deadlift with light load — only if comfortable with small weight like a baby in carrier eventually): 3 sets x 10.
- Side plank full or knees down: 3 sets x 20–30 sec.
- Standing hip abduction with band substitute: 3 x 12–15.
- Finish pelvic floor contraction sequence.

Upper (progress emphasis on scapular & posterior chain)
- Warm up.
- Incline push‑ups (hands on counter) or wall push‑ups: 3 sets x 10–12.
- Seated rows (use resistance band if available; otherwise prone T/Y progressions): 3 sets x 12.
- Overhead press with very light load (water bottles) if comfortable: 3 sets x 10.
- Banded pull‑apart or scapular squeezes: 3 x 15.
- Farmer carry simulation with light load (walking with a baby if comfortable) 2 x 30–60 sec — focus on posture.
- Core integration: Pallof press anti‑rotation with band (or isometric hand press into door frame) 3 x 10–12 sec each side.

Lower B (higher rep/metabolic)
- Warm up.
- Step ups (onto low step): 3 x 12 per leg.
- Reverse lunge to balance: 3 x 10 per leg.
- Single leg RDL bodyweight: 3 x 8–10 per leg.
- Glute bridge hold: 3 x 30–40 sec.
- Calf raises single leg assisted 3 x 10–12.
- Finish with pelvic floor set and diaphragmatic breathing.

Full‑body/core integration
- Warm up.
- Circuit 3 rounds (rest 90 sec between rounds): 10 incline push‑ups; 12 squats; 8 bird‑dogs per side; 12 rows; 30 sec side plank each side. Adjust reps for fatigue. Focus on exhale on exertion and pelvic floor cueing.

Aerobic progressions
- One longer walk 45–60 min at easy pace weekly by week 8 if tolerated.
- Add a brisk interval walk session: 2–3 min brisk/2 min easy x 6–8.

Weeks 9–12 (postpartum weeks 12–15): Strength consolidation and return to regular activity
Goal: Increase intensity, volume, and complexity. Prepare for return to heavier lifting or higher impact if desired and asymptomatic. Introduce more challenging core work, loaded carry variations, and controlled single‑leg strength.

Frequency: 3–4 strength sessions/week (35–50 min), 2–3 aerobic sessions/week.

Progressive options (choose based on goals)
- Add light external load (household weights, water bottles, kettlebell) for squats, hinges, presses if no pelvic symptoms.
- Start more targeted diastasis recti rehab exercises if needed (after pelvic health check): gentle curl progressions like weighted heel slides, dead bug progressions, and eccentric loading with emphasis on tensioning the linea alba without doming.

Example week 12 structure
- Mon: Strength lower (progressed)
  - Goblet squat with light weight: 3 x 8–12
  - Romanian deadlift (light weight) 3 x 8–10
  - Bulgarian split squat 3 x 8 per leg
  - Glute bridges with weight on hips 3 x 10
  - Pelvic floor + breathing cool down
- Wed: Strength upper
  - Push‑ups to knees/progress to floor: 3 x 8–12
  - Bent over row or single arm row: 3 x 8–10
  - Overhead press: 3 x 8–10
  - Loaded carry (farmer carry) 2 x 60 sec
  - Scapular/T spine mobility
- Fri: Full‑body metabolic + core integration
  - Circuit 4 rounds: 30 sec squat to press (light), 30 sec plank or progressive plank (aim toward full plank if ready), 30 sec single‑leg deadlift (bodyweight or light), 30 sec bent over rows — rest 90 sec between rounds.
  - Finish with functional core: dead bug progressions, side plank 30–45 sec.
- Weekend: 1 longer walk or low‑impact cardio 45–60 min.

Return to higher impact (running, heavy lifting)
- Only consider adding running or heavy lifts (squats/deadlifts with challenging loads) after 12 weeks and only if:
  - No pelvic floor symptoms (no leakage, heaviness, bulging)
  - Strong, pain‑free control in single‑leg hops, landing, and higher‑load carries
  - Clearance from provider and ideally assessment from pelvic health PT for diastasis/continence.
- Reintroduce impact gradually (walk/jog intervals starting 30–60 seconds running + 2–3 min walk, monitor symptoms).

Monitoring and progression rules (practical)
- Use the “24‑48 hour rule”: if symptoms (leakage, pressure, bulging, pain) increase after a session, reduce intensity or revert to earlier week’s work for at least one week and refer to pelvic floor physio.
- Load progression: increase reps first, then sets, then add load. Avoid large jumps in intensity.
- Emphasise quality over quantity: proper breath/pelvic floor timing and neutral spine during all lifts.

Nutrition & recovery (brief)
- Protein: aim for ~1.1–1.3 g/kg/day (higher if breastfeeding; many postpartum women benefit from ~20–30 g protein per meal).
- Hydration: especially if breastfeeding — drink to thirst and increase with activity.
- Fiber and stool softener advice: avoid constipation during healing (important for pelvic floor/abdominal strain).
- Sleep hygiene: naps when possible; enlist support for infant care during workouts to allow focused sessions.
- Scar mobilization: once incision fully healed and cleared, gentle scar massage for 1–2 minutes daily can reduce adhesions; only after OB clearance.

When to refer to pelvic health physiotherapist or OB sooner
- Persistent or new urinary/fecal leakage, pain with intercourse, pelvic heaviness, increasing separation or bulge at midline, tenderness at incision, or severe back/hip pain.
- If diastasis recti is present and not improving, or if she plans to return to higher intensity (running, heavy lifting) and needs assessment.

Coaching cues for you as trainer
- Teach diaphragmatic breathing and pelvic floor timing clearly before movement: inhale to prepare, gentle pelvic floor lift and exhale during exertion (no Valsalva).
- Reassure and progress slowly — postpartum recovery is highly individual.
- Keep sessions short and flexible for new parent life; home‑friendly variations and use of household items for light load.

If you want, I can:
- Convert this into a printable week‑by‑week sheet with exact daily sessions and checklists.
- Provide progressions/regressions for specific exercises (e.g., how to scale a single‑leg deadlift or modify core moves safely).
- Create a more detailed nutrition plan tailored to her weight/goals and breastfeeding status.

Would you like a printable calendar version or exercise demonstration cues for any of the movements?
